2-1.bio:
St. Tryphon was born in the village of Campsada in Phrygia, in Asia Minor, where as a youth he tended geese. Endowed by God with grace to heal the sick and drive out evil spirits, he became known far beyond his village. During the persecution of Decius in the third century he confessed Christ, endured torture, and was condemned to death, receiving the martyr's crown while still young.

The faithful invoke him as a protector of gardens, fields, and vineyards, and his blessing is asked over crops against every pest. He is commemorated on February 1.
2-1.name: Tryphon

2-1.bio:
St. Perpetua was a young noblewoman of Carthage, a nursing mother, who was imprisoned together with her servant Felicity and the catechumens Saturus, Revocatus, Saturninus and Secundulus during the persecution under Septimius Severus. Felicity gave birth in prison shortly before the group was led into the arena.

The account of their martyrdom, partly written by Perpetua herself, is among the earliest Christian martyrdom narratives. They were thrown to wild beasts and then slain by the sword in Carthage at the beginning of the third century.
2-1.desc: Holy Martyrs Perpetua and Felicity of Carthage, with the catechumens Saturus, Revocatus, Saturninus and Secundulus.
2-1.name: Perpetua and Felicity of Carthage

2-1.bio:
St. Peter of Galatia left his home while still a boy and lived as a hermit, first in Galatia and later near Antioch in Syria, where Theodoret of Cyrrhus knew him and recorded his life. He spent his days in fasting, prayer and silence in a small tomb-like cell.

Tradition relates that he received the gift of healing and delivered many from illness and demonic affliction, reposing in peace at a great age.
2-1.desc: Venerable Peter the Hermit of Galatia, ascetic near Antioch.
2-1.name: Peter of Galatia

2-1.bio:
St. Vendemianos came from Mysia and became a disciple of St. Auxentios on the mountain near Chalcedon. After the death of his elder he continued to live in a cleft of the rock on Mount Oxia, struggling in fasting and prayer for many decades.

He was granted the gift of working miracles and reposed in peace in the early sixth century.
2-1.desc: Venerable Vendemianos, hermit of Mount Oxia in Bithynia and disciple of St. Auxentios.
2-1.name: Vendemianos of Bithynia

2-1.bio:
St. Anastasios was a painter from Nafplio in the Peloponnese. Tradition relates that after a broken betrothal he was driven out of his senses and in that state was drawn into professing Islam; when he came to himself he publicly renounced it and confessed Christ before the Turkish authorities.

He was cut down by the crowd and received the crown of martyrdom in Nafplio at the beginning of the eighteenth century.
2-1.desc: New Martyr Anastasios the painter of Nafplio, who suffered under the Ottomans.
2-1.name: Anastasios of Nafplio

2-1.bio:
St. Brigid was born in Ireland in the fifth century and from childhood was known for her generosity to the poor. She received the monastic veil and founded the great monastery of Kildare, which became a centre of learning and charity.

Honoured as the Mary of the Gael, she is counted with Patrick and Columba among the three patrons of Ireland and is venerated as a pre-schism saint of the undivided Church.
2-1.desc: Venerable Brigid of Kildare, abbess and enlightener of Ireland.
2-1.name: Brigid of Ireland

2-1.bio:
St. Basil was Archbishop of Thessaloniki during the period of iconoclasm. He stood firm in the veneration of the holy icons and endured persecution for the Orthodox faith, earning the title of Confessor.

He reposed in peace in the ninth century, having shepherded his flock through a time of great trial.
2-1.desc: St. Basil the Confessor, Archbishop of Thessaloniki, defender of the holy icons.
2-1.name: Basil the Confessor of Thessaloniki

2-10.bio:
St. Charalambos was a priest of Magnesia in Asia Minor who suffered martyrdom in extreme old age, according to tradition at the age of 113, during the persecutions of the early third century. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, he endured torture with such serenity that many who witnessed his suffering came to believe in Christ.

He is among the most beloved saints of Greece, where countless churches bear his name. The faithful have long invoked him as a protector against sickness and plague, and as a guardian of flocks and fields. His feast is celebrated on February 10.
2-10.desc: Holy Martyr Charalambos of Magnesia, patron against illness.
2-10.name: Charalambos

2-10.bio:
St. Zeno was born to a noble family of Caesarea in Cappadocia and served as an imperial courier under the Emperor Valens. After the emperor's death he left the world and lived as a hermit in a tomb near Antioch, in extreme poverty and silence.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who visited him, records his life; he reposed in peace in the early fifth century.
2-10.desc: Venerable Zeno the Courier, hermit near Antioch, former servant of the Emperor Valens.
2-10.name: Zeno the Faster

2-10.bio:
Porphyrios and Baptos were the soldiers ordered to torture St. Charalambos. Seeing his miraculous endurance, they confessed Christ and were beheaded with him.

They are commemorated with three women who also came to faith through the saint's sufferings.
2-10.desc: Holy Martyrs Porphyrios and Baptos, the executioners who believed through St. Charalambos.
2-10.name: Porphyrios and Baptos

2-10.bio:
Ennatha of Gaza, Valentina of Caesarea and Paula of Palestine were young Christian women arrested during the persecution under Maximinus. Ennatha rebuked the governor Firmilian for his idolatry, and Valentina overturned the pagan altar.

All three were tortured and burned or beheaded at Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century.
2-10.desc: Virgin Martyrs Ennatha, Valentina and Paula of Palestine.
2-10.name: Ennatha, Valentina and Paula

2-10.bio: St. Anastasios was Patriarch of Jerusalem in the fifth century and is honoured among the holy hierarchs of the Holy City. He governed the Church of Jerusalem in a time of doctrinal turmoil and reposed in peace.
2-10.name: Anastasios of Jerusalem

2-10.bio:
St. Anna was a Swedish princess, Ingigerd, who married Great Prince Yaroslav the Wise of Kiev and raised her many children in Christian piety. In later life she took monastic vows in Novgorod.

She reposed in the eleventh century and is buried in the Cathedral of Holy Wisdom in Novgorod.
2-10.desc: Venerable Anna of Novgorod, princess, wife of Yaroslav the Wise.
2-10.name: Anna of Novgorod

2-10.bio:
St. Prochoros came from Smolensk and became a monk at the Kiev Caves, where he ate only bread made from the wild orach plant. During a famine he baked this bread for the hungry, and it tasted sweet to those who took it with a blessing.

He also miraculously turned ashes into salt for the people during a shortage. He reposed in the early twelfth century.
2-10.desc: Venerable Prochoros the Wonderworker of the Kiev Caves, called the Orach-eater.
2-10.name: Prochoros of the Kiev Caves

2-11.bio:
St. Blaise was Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, a physician of both bodies and souls. During the persecutions of the early fourth century he was seized, and after enduring tortures for his confession of Christ he was beheaded. Tradition tells of his kindness even to wild beasts, and of a boy saved from choking through his prayer.

For this the faithful have long invoked him for ailments of the throat, and his veneration spread widely in both East and West. He is commemorated on February 11.
2-11.name: Blaise

2-11.bio:
St. Theodora was the wife of the iconoclast Emperor Theophilos. Throughout his reign she secretly venerated the holy icons, and after his death, ruling as regent for her son Michael, she convened the council of 843 that restored the icons to the churches, an event celebrated each year as the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

In later life she was removed from power and lived in a monastery, where she reposed in peace; her relics are venerated in Corfu.
2-11.desc: Righteous Empress Theodora, who restored the veneration of the holy icons.
2-11.name: Theodora the Empress

2-11.bio:
St. George was born in Kratovo and learned the goldsmith's trade. After his father's death he moved to Sofia, where a Muslim scholar tried to persuade him to embrace Islam. George answered with a bold defence of the Christian faith.

He was brought before the judge, refused every inducement, and was burned alive in Sofia in 1515, at the age of eighteen.
2-11.desc: New Martyr George of Kratovo, goldsmith, burned alive in Sofia.
2-11.name: George of Kratovo

2-11.bio:
St. Demetrios was born to a wealthy merchant family of Pereslavl and became a monk in his youth. He was a friend of St. Sergius of Radonezh and, seeking solitude, went north to Vologda, where he founded the Monastery of the Saviour at Priluki.

He was known for his strict fasting and his charity, and reposed in peace in the fourteenth century.
2-11.desc: Venerable Demetrios of Priluki, wonderworker of Vologda.
2-11.name: Demetrios of Priluki

2-11.bio:
St. Vsevolod, grandson of Vladimir Monomakh, ruled Novgorod and later Pskov in the twelfth century. He was known for his justice, his generosity to the poor and his building of churches, including the Cathedral of the Holy Trinity in Pskov.

He reposed in 1138 and is venerated as the heavenly protector of Pskov.
2-11.desc: Right-believing Prince Vsevolod, in baptism Gabriel, wonderworker of Pskov.
2-11.name: Vsevolod-Gabriel of Pskov

2-12.bio:
St. Meletios was Archbishop of Antioch in the fourth century, a gentle and steadfast champion of the Nicene faith. For his defense of the divinity of Christ against the Arians he was driven from his see into exile more than once, yet he never ceased to shepherd his flock in patience and peace.

Restored at last, he presided at the opening of the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople in 381, and reposed in the Lord while the council was in session, mourned by the whole Church. He is commemorated on February 12.
2-12.desc: Archbishop of Antioch, champion of Orthodoxy.
2-12.name: Meletios of Antioch

2-12.bio:
St. Mary followed her widowed father Eugene into a monastery in Bithynia disguised as a young man, taking the name Marinos. Falsely accused of fathering a child, she accepted the blame in silence and was expelled from the monastery, raising the child at its gate in great poverty.

Only after her death was her innocence and her true identity discovered, and the monks glorified God for her humility.
2-12.desc: Venerable Mary, who lived as the monk Marinos in a monastery of Bithynia.
2-12.name: Mary called Marinos

2-12.bio:
St. Christos came from Albania and worked as a gardener in Constantinople. After a quarrel with a Turk over the price of apples, he was falsely accused of having promised to become a Muslim and was thrown into prison.

He refused to deny Christ despite hunger and torture, and was beheaded in Constantinople in 1748.
2-12.desc: New Martyr Christos the Gardener of Albania, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-12.name: Christos the Gardener

2-12.bio:
St. Antonios was born near Constantinople to pious parents and became a monk at the age of twelve. Known for his asceticism and love for the poor, he was made abbot and later Patriarch of Constantinople in the late ninth century.

He worked to heal the divisions in the Church that followed the deposition of St. Photios and reposed in peace.
2-12.desc: St. Antonios Kauleas, Patriarch of Constantinople.
2-12.name: Antonios of Constantinople

2-12.bio:
St. Alexis was born to a noble family and became a monk in Moscow in his youth. Consecrated Metropolitan of Kiev and All Russia in the fourteenth century, he guided the Russian state during the minority of Prince Dimitri Donskoy and was a close friend of St. Sergius of Radonezh.

Tradition relates that he healed the Tatar khan's wife of blindness. He reposed in 1378 and his relics rest in Moscow.
2-12.desc: St. Alexis, Metropolitan of Moscow, wonderworker of All Russia.
2-12.name: Alexis of Moscow

2-12.bio:
St. Meletios was born in the village of Lardos on Rhodes in the late eighteenth century and baptised Emmanuel. He became a monk and, tradition relates, found an icon of the Theotokos at Ypseni, where he built a monastery that became a spiritual centre of the island.

Slandered and persecuted in his old age, he bore all with patience and reposed in peace in the nineteenth century.
2-12.desc: Venerable Meletios of Lardos, founder of the Monastery of Ypseni in Rhodes.
2-12.name: Meletios of Ypseni

2-13.bio:
St. Martinian was a hermit of the region of Caesarea in Palestine, who took up the ascetic life as a young man and dwelt for many years in the desert in prayer and fasting. Tradition tells of the fierce struggles he endured against temptation, and of the lengths to which he went to preserve his purity, fleeing at last to a bare rock in the sea and then wandering from place to place with no home but Christ.

He ended his days in peace, an example of vigilance and repentance. He is commemorated on February 13.
2-13.desc: Venerable Martinian the Hermit of Caesarea.
2-13.name: Martinian

2-13.bio:
Aquila, a Jew of Pontus, and his wife Priscilla were tentmakers living in Corinth when St. Paul came to lodge and work with them. They accompanied him to Ephesus, instructed Apollos in the faith, and opened their home as a church.

St. Paul greets them warmly in his epistles as those who risked their necks for his life; tradition relates that they ended their lives as martyrs.
2-13.desc: Holy Apostles Aquila and Priscilla, fellow-workers of St. Paul.
2-13.name: Aquila and Priscilla

2-13.bio:
St. Eulogios was abbot of a monastery in Antioch before being elected Patriarch of Alexandria in the late sixth century. A friend and correspondent of St. Gregory the Great of Rome, he combated the Monophysite and other heresies with his writings.

He governed the Church of Alexandria for many years and reposed in peace in the early seventh century.
2-13.name: Eulogios of Alexandria

2-13.bio:
St. Symeon was Stefan Nemanja, the Grand Prince who united the Serbian lands in the twelfth century. Late in life he abdicated in favour of his son and joined his youngest son St. Sava on Mount Athos, where together they founded the Monastery of Chilandar.

He reposed there in 1199, and his relics flowed with myrrh, earning him the title Myrrh-streaming.
2-13.desc: Venerable Symeon the Myrrh-streaming, Stefan Nemanja, founder of Chilandar on Mount Athos.
2-13.name: Symeon the Myrrh-streaming

2-13.bio:
St. Seraphima, born Euphemia Morgacheva in the Ryazan region in the nineteenth century, devoted herself from youth to prayer and fasting. She became a disciple of the recluse John of Sezenovo and later guided the women's community that grew up there.

She reposed in peace in 1877, revered for her ascetic life and spiritual counsel.
2-13.desc: Venerable Seraphima of Sezenovo, ascetic of Russia.
2-13.name: Seraphima of Sezenovo

2-13.bio:
St. George was born in Nezhin in the eighteenth century, studied at the Kiev academy and became a monk of the Kiev Caves Lavra. As Archbishop of Mogilev he defended the Orthodox faithful of Belarus against Uniate pressure and worked for the education of the clergy.

He reposed in 1795, honoured as a confessor of Orthodoxy in the western lands.
2-13.desc: St. George Konissky, Archbishop of Mogilev in Belarus.
2-13.name: George of Mogilev

2-14.bio:
St. Auxentios lived in the fifth century and served for a time at the imperial court in Constantinople before forsaking the world for the life of a hermit. He settled on a mountain in Bithynia, not far from Chalcedon, where he lived in a small cell in fasting and prayer, receiving the many who climbed to him for counsel and healing.

He upheld the Orthodox faith of the Council of Chalcedon and was revered as a discerning elder and wonderworker. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on February 14.
2-14.name: Auxentios

2-14.bio:
St. Maron lived in the open air on a mountain near Cyrrhus in Syria, where he turned a former pagan temple into a place of prayer. Theodoret records that he received the gift of healing and delivered many from illness and demons.

He trained a great number of ascetics, among them St. James of Cyrrhus, and reposed in peace in the early fifth century.
2-14.desc: Venerable Maron, hermit of Syria, teacher of many ascetics.
2-14.name: Maron the Hermit

2-14.bio:
Two martyrs named Valentine are commemorated on this day: a presbyter of Rome and the Bishop of Terni in Italy, both of whom suffered in the third century. Tradition relates that they healed the sick and brought many to Christ, for which they were arrested and beheaded.

The Church of the East and West honoured them together long before the schism; their relics were venerated in Rome.
2-14.desc: Hieromartyr Valentine, presbyter of Rome, and Valentine, Bishop of Terni.
2-14.name: Valentine the Hieromartyr

2-14.bio:
St. George, called Paizanos, was born on the island of Lesvos and worked as a tailor. Tradition relates that he was denounced to the Turkish authorities in Constantinople and pressed to change his faith.

He confessed Christ steadfastly and was put to death in Constantinople in 1693.
2-14.desc: New Martyr George Paizanos of Lesvos, tailor, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-14.name: George Paizanos of Mytilene

2-14.bio:
St. Nicholas was born in the village of Psari in Corinthia and, orphaned young, went to Selymbria where he married, and later worked as a grocer in Constantinople. Falsely accused of having accepted Islam, he was imprisoned and tortured.

He refused to deny Christ and was beheaded in Constantinople in 1554.
2-14.desc: New Martyr Nicholas of Psari in Corinthia, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-14.name: Nicholas of Psari

2-14.bio:
St. Nicholas came from Trebizond and lived in the region of Amaseia in Pontus. From youth he wished to dedicate himself to God, and after the death of his wife and child he became a priest and served the faithful with zeal.

He was seized by the Turks, refused to renounce his faith, and received the crown of martyrdom.
2-14.desc: Hieromartyr Nicholas of Trebizond, priest of Pontus.
2-14.name: Nicholas of Trebizond

2-14.bio: St. Philemon, Bishop of Gaza, is recorded in an early Patmian manuscript as a hieromartyr of the Church. No further details of his life have been preserved.
2-14.name: Philemon of Gaza

2-15.bio:
St. Onesimos the Apostle was the slave of Philemon of Colossae who fled from his master and, by God's providence, came to St. Paul in his imprisonment. There he was converted, and Paul sent him back with the Epistle to Philemon, asking that he be received no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother in Christ.

Numbered among the Seventy Apostles, he later served the Church in the preaching of the Gospel, and according to tradition he ended his life as a martyr. He is commemorated on February 15.
2-15.desc: Holy Apostle Onesimos, disciple of Paul.
2-15.name: Onesimos

2-15.bio:
St. Anthimos was born on Chios in 1869 to a poor family and from youth was drawn to prayer and the ascetic life. He became a monk and priest and, tradition relates, was granted the gifts of healing and spiritual discernment, ministering for years among the lepers of Chios.

He founded the Convent of Panagia Voithia (Our Lady the Helper) on Chios, where he served as spiritual father, and reposed in 1960.
2-15.desc: Venerable Anthimos Vagianos of Chios, founder of the Convent of Panagia Voithia.
2-15.name: Anthimos of Chios

2-15.bio:
St. Eusebios lived on a mountainside in Syria in the fourth century, exposed to heat and cold, clothed in skins and eating almost nothing. Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who describes his life, marvelled at his endurance.

He reposed in peace at a great age, an example of the extreme asceticism of the Syrian desert.
2-15.name: Eusebios the Hermit

2-15.bio:
St. John came from Koulakia, the present-day Chalastra near Thessaloniki, and was a teacher. For a time he lived on Mount Athos before returning to the world.

Denounced to the Turks, he confessed Christ with courage and was hanged in Thessaloniki in the eighteenth century.
2-15.desc: New Martyr John of Koulakia, teacher, who suffered in Thessaloniki.
2-15.name: John Koulakiotis

2-15.bio:
St. Maior was a soldier serving in Gaza during the persecution of Diocletian. Denounced as a Christian, he confessed Christ before the governor with boldness.

He was scourged and tortured for many days and gave up his soul to God, in the early fourth century.
2-15.desc: Holy Martyr Maior, soldier, who suffered at Gaza.
2-15.name: Maior the Martyr

2-15.bio:
Chloe, Crispus, Justus and Titius are mentioned in the New Testament as members of the church of Corinth and companions of the Apostle Paul: Crispus was ruler of the synagogue whom Paul baptised, Titius Justus opened his house next to it, and Chloe's household sent word to Paul about the divisions in the community.

Their memory is kept in Ancient Corinth on the Sunday after February 13.
2-15.desc: Sts. Chloe, Crispus, Justus and Titius, fellow-workers of the Apostle Paul in Corinth.
2-15.name: Chloe, Crispus, Justus and Titius of Corinth

2-16.bio:
St. Pamphilos was a priest of Caesarea in Palestine, a man of great learning who devoted his life to the study and careful copying of the Holy Scriptures and gathered a famous library for the Church. During the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century he was imprisoned for his confession of Christ, and after a long captivity he was put to death together with a company of fellow martyrs.

The historian Eusebius, who loved him as a friend and teacher, preserved his memory for the whole Church. He is commemorated on February 16.
2-16.name: Pamphilos

2-16.bio:
St. Flavian was Patriarch of Constantinople in the fifth century. He condemned the heresy of Eutyches at a local council, but at the Robber Council of Ephesus in 449 he was deposed and so brutally beaten by the heretics that he died shortly afterwards.

The Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon vindicated his memory and his relics were brought to Constantinople with honour.
2-16.desc: St. Flavian the Confessor, Patriarch of Constantinople.
2-16.name: Flavian of Constantinople

2-16.bio:
St. Marouthas was a learned bishop of Mesopotamia who served as envoy between the Byzantine and Persian courts and won the favour of the Persian king, securing relief for the persecuted Christians. He gathered the relics of the Persian martyrs into his city, which was thereafter called Martyropolis.

He wrote an account of their sufferings and reposed in peace in the early fifth century.
2-16.desc: St. Marouthas, Bishop of Martyropolis, and the Persian Martyrs whose relics he gathered.
2-16.name: Marouthas of Martyropolis

2-16.bio:
St. Romanos came from Karpenisi in central Greece. Tradition relates that he was a simple, illiterate man who longed for martyrdom, became a monk on Mount Athos and was prepared for his contest by the fathers there.

He went to Constantinople, confessed Christ before the Turkish authorities, and was beheaded in the late seventeenth century.
2-16.desc: New Monk-martyr Romanos of Karpenisi, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-16.name: Romanos the New Martyr

2-17.bio:
St. Theodore the Recruit, called Teron, was a young soldier in Asia Minor during the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, he boldly confessed Christ, and after imprisonment and torture he was given over to death by fire, sealing his faith as a Great Martyr.

The Church also remembers his help after death: through him the faithful were warned to keep from food defiled by idols, and in his memory kolyva is blessed on the first Saturday of Great Lent. His feast is kept on February 17.
2-17.name: Theodore of Tyre

2-17.bio:
St. Pulcheria, daughter of the Emperor Arcadius, was proclaimed Augusta in her youth and guided the empire during the reign of her brother Theodosius II, living in virginity and piety. After his death she married the general Marcian, who ruled with her in chastity.

Together they convened the Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon in 451, which condemned the Monophysite heresy. Pulcheria built many churches of the Theotokos in Constantinople and reposed in 453.
2-17.desc: Holy right-believing Emperor Marcian and Empress Pulcheria, who convened the Fourth Ecumenical Council.
2-17.name: Marcian and Pulcheria

2-17.bio:
St. Mariamne was the sister of the Apostle Philip and shared in his preaching together with the Apostle Bartholomew, travelling through Asia Minor and enduring persecution at Hierapolis. After her brother's martyrdom she continued to preach in Lycaonia.

She reposed in peace, honoured by the Church as Equal-to-the-Apostles.
2-17.desc: St. Mariamne, Equal-to-the-Apostles, sister of the Apostle Philip.
2-17.name: Mariamne the Equal-to-the-Apostles

2-17.bio:
St. Auxibios was born to a wealthy pagan family of Rome and, refusing the marriage arranged for him, sailed to Cyprus, where he was baptised by the Apostle Mark and later consecrated Bishop of Soli by St. Herakleidios.

He converted many pagans and reposed in peace in the first century; his shrine in Cyprus remains a place of veneration.
2-17.desc: St. Auxibios, Bishop of Soli in Cyprus.
2-17.name: Auxibios of Soli

2-17.bio:
St. Theodore was born in Neochori near Constantinople and as a young man worked in the Sultan's palace, where he was drawn into professing Islam. Repenting bitterly, he confessed Christ openly in Mytilene before the Turkish judge.

He endured imprisonment and torture and was hanged in Mytilene in 1795, where his relics are venerated.
2-17.desc: New Martyr Theodore of Neochori in Constantinople, who suffered in Mytilene.
2-17.name: Theodore the Byzantine

2-17.bio:
St. Hermogenes served as a priest in Kazan, where he witnessed the finding of the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God, and later became Metropolitan of Kazan and Patriarch of Moscow. During the Time of Troubles he called the Russian people to resist the Polish occupation and refused to sanction a Catholic ruler.

Imprisoned by the invaders in the Kremlin, he died of starvation in 1612, honoured as a martyr for faith and nation.
2-17.desc: Hieromartyr Hermogenes, Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia.
2-17.name: Hermogenes of Moscow

2-17.bio:
St. Agathangelos was a young shoemaker from Florina in Macedonia who worked in Bitola. Grieved by the forced conversions of Christians during the Muslim festivals, he obtained an imperial decree from Constantinople to stop them.

For this he was seized by the Turks of Bitola, refused to deny Christ, and was put to death in the eighteenth century.
2-17.desc: New Martyr Agathangelos of Florina, shoemaker, who suffered in Bitola.
2-17.name: Agathangelos of Florina

2-18.bio:
St. Leo the Great was Pope of Rome in the fifth century, one of the great fathers of the undivided Church. His celebrated Tome, read at the Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon in 451, confessed with clarity that Christ is one Person in two natures, true God and true man, and the fathers of the council received it as the voice of Peter.

He shepherded Rome through perilous times, and tradition tells that he turned Attila the Hun away from the city. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on February 18.
2-18.desc: Pope Leo the Great of Rome.
2-18.name: Leo the Great

2-18.bio:
Sts. Leo and Paregorios were close friends in Patara of Lycia. Paregorios was arrested first and martyred after many tortures. Leo, weeping at the place of his friend's death, was moved to smash the lamps of a pagan temple and openly confess Christ.

He was dragged over rocks and slain, joining his friend in the crown of martyrdom in the third century.
2-18.desc: Holy Martyrs Leo and Paregorios of Patara in Lycia.
2-18.name: Leo and Paregorios of Patara

2-18.bio:
St. Agapitos was born in Cappadocia and became a monk in his youth, famed for his asceticism and his miracles. Forced into military service under Licinius, he was wounded for his faith, then released and ordained; the Emperor Constantine later made him Bishop of Synnada.

He shepherded his flock with love, healing the sick by his prayers, and reposed in peace in the fourth century.
2-18.desc: St. Agapitos the Confessor and Wonderworker, Bishop of Synnada in Phrygia.
2-18.name: Agapitos of Synnada

2-18.bio: Sts. Agrippas, Victorinos, Dorotheos and Theodoulos confessed Christ and were put to death for the faith. The Synaxaria record only the fact of their martyrdom.
2-18.desc: Holy Martyrs Agrippas, Victorinos, Dorotheos and Theodoulos.
2-18.name: Agrippas, Victorinos, Dorotheos and Theodoulos

2-18.bio:
St. Cosmas was the servant of a boyar whom he nursed through a long illness. Tradition relates that at the river Yakhrom an icon of the Dormition of the Theotokos appeared to him and healed his master.

He became a monk at the Kiev Caves and later returned to the Yakhrom, where he founded a monastery in honour of the Dormition and reposed in the fifteenth century.
2-18.desc: Venerable Cosmas of Yakhrom, founder of the Dormition Monastery.
2-18.name: Cosmas of Yakhrom

2-19.bio:
St. Archippos the Apostle is named in the New Testament, where St. Paul calls him his fellow soldier and bids him fulfill the ministry he received in the Lord. Numbered among the Seventy Apostles, he served the church at Colossae in the household of Philemon in the earliest days of the faith.

According to tradition he sealed his ministry with martyrdom, suffering for Christ in the time of the persecutions. He is commemorated on February 19.
2-19.name: Archippos

2-19.bio:
St. Philothei was born in Athens in the sixteenth century to a noble family, and after the death of her husband devoted herself and her wealth to God. She founded a convent dedicated to St. Andrew in Athens, together with schools, hospices and workshops, and ransomed Christian women from Turkish captivity.

Her charity aroused the anger of the Turks, who beat her savagely; she died of her wounds in 1589 and is honoured as the patroness of Athens, where her relics rest in the Metropolitan Cathedral.
2-19.desc: Venerable Martyr Philothei of Athens, foundress and protectress of the city.
2-19.name: Philothei of Athens

2-19.bio:
St. Nikitas was born in Epirus and became a hieromonk at the Skete of St. Anne on Mount Athos. Burning with zeal for the faith, he set out to preach to the Muslims and was arrested near Serres.

After enduring cruel tortures he was hanged in Serres in 1808.
2-19.desc: New Hieromartyr Nikitas of Epirus, hieromonk of Mount Athos, who suffered at Serres.
2-19.name: Nikitas the New Hieromartyr

2-19.bio:
Sts. Maximos, Theodotos, Hesychios and the maiden Asklepiodote were arrested at Adrianople in Thrace during the persecution of Maximian. They were tied to trees and torn with iron hooks, but remained steadfast in their confession.

Tradition relates that their prayers worked miracles that brought many to faith before they were beheaded in the early fourth century.
2-19.desc: Holy Martyrs Maximos, Theodotos, Hesychios and Asklepiodote of Adrianople.
2-19.name: Maximos, Theodotos, Hesychios and Asklepiodote

2-19.bio:
Sts. Eugene and Makarios were presbyters of Antioch who boldly rebuked the Emperor Julian the Apostate for his rejection of Christ. They were scourged and exiled to the Arabian desert.

There they lived as ascetics on a mountain, driving out the demons that dwelt there, and reposed in peace in the fourth century.
2-19.desc: Venerable Confessors Eugene and Makarios, presbyters of Antioch.
2-19.name: Eugene and Makarios the Confessors

2-19.bio:
St. Raboulas was born in Samosata and became a monk in his youth, living in asceticism in Syria and Phoenicia. He later came to Constantinople, where the Emperor Zeno built a monastery for him.

He converted many pagans and reposed in peace at a great age in the early sixth century.
2-19.desc: Venerable Raboulas of Samosata, ascetic and founder of monasteries.
2-19.name: Raboulas of Samosata

2-2.bio:
Forty days after His Nativity, the infant Christ was brought to the Temple in Jerusalem by the Theotokos and the righteous Joseph, in fulfillment of the Law of Moses. There He was received into the arms of the Elder Simeon, to whom it had been revealed that he would not die before seeing the Messiah, and Simeon blessed God with the prayer now sung at every Vespers. The aged Prophetess Anna likewise gave thanks and spoke of the Child to all who awaited redemption.

This Great Feast, called in Greek the Ypapanti, the Meeting, celebrates the encounter of the Old Covenant with the New, and is kept on February 2.
2-2.desc: Meeting of Our Lord Jesus Christ in the Temple — 40 days after Nativity.
2-2.name: Presentation of the Lord

2-2.bio:
St. Jordan came from Trebizond in Pontus and settled with his family in Galata in Constantinople. When a Muslim companion mocked St. Nicholas, Jordan answered with a bold word in defence of the saint and was denounced for insulting Islam.

He refused every offer to save his life by changing his faith and was beheaded in Constantinople in the seventeenth century.
2-2.desc: New Martyr Jordan of Trebizond, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-2.name: Jordan of Trebizond

2-2.bio:
St. Gabriel came from Alone on the island of Prokonnesos. He became a monk and served as a preacher in Constantinople. Accused of insulting the Muslim religion, he was imprisoned and tortured.

He remained steadfast in his confession of Christ and was put to death in Constantinople in the seventeenth century.
2-2.desc: Monk-martyr Gabriel of Prokonnesos, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-2.name: Gabriel of Prokonnesos

2-2.bio: St. Agathodoros is commemorated among the martyrs of the early Church. The Synaxaria relate only that he confessed Christ and was slain, receiving the crown of martyrdom.
2-2.desc: Holy Martyr Agathodoros, who completed his contest by the sword.
2-2.name: Agathodoros the Martyr

2-20.bio:
St. Leo was Bishop of Catania in Sicily in the eighth century, a shepherd remembered for his mercy toward the poor and the sick, and honored as a wonderworker for the healings granted through his prayers. Tradition also tells of his boldness in confronting a notorious sorcerer who was leading the people astray, whose deceptions collapsed before the bishop's faith.

He reposed in peace, and his relics were venerated in his city. He is commemorated on February 20.
2-20.name: Leo of Catania

2-20.bio:
St. Agathon was born in Sicily, gave his inheritance to the poor and became a monk. Elected Bishop of Rome in 678, he sent legates to the Sixth Ecumenical Council in Constantinople, which condemned the Monothelite heresy in accordance with his confession of faith.

He was known for his gentleness and his gift of healing, and reposed in peace in 681.
2-20.desc: St. Agathon, Pope of Rome, defender of Orthodoxy against Monothelitism.
2-20.name: Agathon of Rome

2-20.bio:
St. Bessarion was an Egyptian who became a disciple of St. Anthony the Great and St. Makarios and lived as a wanderer in the desert, owning nothing and sleeping in the open. The Sayings of the Desert Fathers preserve his words and record that he stood forty days and nights in prayer without sleep.

He was granted the gift of miracles, including walking across the Nile and turning salt water sweet, and reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-20.desc: Venerable Bessarion the Great, wonderworker of Egypt.
2-20.name: Bessarion the Great

2-20.bio:
St. Sadok succeeded the hieromartyr Symeon as bishop in Persia during the persecution of King Shapur II. Tradition relates that he was warned of his coming martyrdom in a dream by his predecessor.

Arrested with 128 of his clergy and faithful, he refused to worship the sun and was beheaded with them in the fourth century.
2-20.desc: Hieromartyr Sadok, Bishop of Persia, and the 128 Martyrs with him.
2-20.name: Sadok and the 128 Martyrs

2-20.bio:
St. Apphia is greeted by the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to Philemon as a beloved fellow-Christian; tradition holds her to be the wife of Philemon, in whose house at Colossae the Church gathered.

She suffered martyrdom together with her husband when pagans broke into the church during a festival and stoned the faithful, in the first century.
2-20.desc: Holy Martyr Apphia, wife of the Apostle Philemon.
2-20.name: Apphia the Martyr

2-20.bio:
St. Cornelius was born in Pskov in 1501 to a noble family and became a monk at the Pskov Caves Monastery, where he was later elected abbot. Under his leadership the monastery flourished, its walls were built and missions were sent to the neighbouring Estonian peoples.

Tradition relates that Tsar Ivan the Terrible, suspecting him of treason, struck him down at the monastery gate in 1570 and immediately repented, carrying the body inside himself.
2-20.desc: Venerable Martyr Cornelius, Abbot of the Pskov Caves Monastery.
2-20.name: Cornelius of the Pskov Caves

2-21.bio:
St. Timothy of Symbola was a monk who lived the ascetic life at the monastery of Symbola in Bithynia, in Asia Minor. From his youth he embraced obedience, fasting, and unceasing prayer, and the synaxaria remember him as a vessel of purity who received from God grace to heal the sick and drive away evil spirits.

Having lived to old age in holiness, he reposed in peace. He is commemorated on February 21.
2-21.name: Timothy of Symbola

2-21.bio:
St. Eustathios was born in Side of Pamphylia and became Bishop of Beroea and then Archbishop of Antioch. He took a leading part in the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 325, defending the divinity of Christ against Arius.

The Arians later deposed him on false charges and he died in exile in Thrace; his relics were brought back to Antioch with great honour in the fifth century.
2-21.desc: St. Eustathios the Confessor, Archbishop of Antioch, Father of the First Ecumenical Council.
2-21.name: Eustathios of Antioch

2-21.bio:
St. John was born near Antioch and trained as a lawyer before becoming a priest. He compiled an early collection of the canons of the Church and was raised to the patriarchal throne of Constantinople in the sixth century.

He governed the Church for twelve years and reposed in peace.
2-21.desc: St. John III Scholastikos, Patriarch of Constantinople, compiler of the canons.
2-21.name: John Scholastikos

2-21.bio:
St. Zacharias was Patriarch of Jerusalem when the Persians captured the city in 614. He was taken into captivity together with the Precious Cross and many of the faithful, and consoled his flock through years of exile.

He returned to Jerusalem with the Cross after the victory of the Emperor Heraclius and reposed in peace.
2-21.desc: St. Zacharias, Patriarch of Jerusalem, who was led captive to Persia.
2-21.name: Zacharias of Jerusalem

2-21.bio:
St. George was born near Amastris in Paphlagonia to pious parents and became a hermit and later a monk. Against his will he was chosen Bishop of Amastris, where he was known for his charity and his miracles.

Tradition relates that after his death his intercession saved the city from a raid by the Rus'. He reposed in the early ninth century.
2-21.desc: St. George, Bishop of Amastris on the Black Sea, wonderworker.
2-21.name: George of Amastris

2-21.bio: Sts. Andrew and Anatolios were disciples of St. Euthymios the Great in the Judaean desert. They followed the way of their elder in fasting, vigil and prayer and reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-21.desc: Venerable Andrew and Anatolios, disciples of St. Euthymios the Great.
2-21.name: Andrew and Anatolios

2-22.bio:
St. Athanasius the Confessor was a monk who lived in the time of the iconoclast persecutions, when the emperors made war upon the holy images. For his steadfast veneration of the icons of Christ and His saints he endured affliction and persecution, bearing witness to the Orthodox faith without wavering.

Having confessed the truth to the end, he reposed in peace, and the Church numbers him among the confessors who preserved the veneration of the holy icons. He is commemorated on February 22.
2-22.name: Athanasius the Confessor

2-22.bio:
During the reign of the Emperor Arcadius the incorrupt relics of many unnamed martyrs were found buried near the Gate of Eugenios in Constantinople. Miracles of healing took place at their discovery.

Tradition relates that among them were the relics of the Apostle Andronikos and his companion Junia, and a church was built over the site.
2-22.desc: Finding of the relics of the Holy Martyrs at the Gate of Eugenios in Constantinople.
2-22.name: Martyrs at the Gate of Eugenios

2-22.bio: St. Anthousa and the twelve servants of her household confessed Christ together and were beheaded. The Synaxaria record only the fact of their martyrdom.
2-22.desc: Holy Martyr Anthousa and her twelve servants, who suffered by the sword.
2-22.name: Anthousa and her Twelve Servants

2-22.bio:
St. Thalassios lived for many years on a hilltop near Cyrrhus in Syria without any shelter, known for his gentleness and humility. His disciple Limnaios later lived with St. Maron and then in a stone enclosure open to the sky, where he cared for the blind and the poor.

Both are described by Theodoret of Cyrrhus and reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-22.desc: Venerable Thalassios and Limnaios, hermits of Syria.
2-22.name: Thalassios and Limnaios

2-22.bio:
St. Baradatos lived near Antioch in a tiny stone cell without door or window, and later stood in the open dressed in skins, raising his hands to heaven in unceasing prayer. Theodoret praised his wisdom and understanding.

He reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-22.name: Baradatos of Syria

2-22.bio:
St. Telesphoros was a Greek who became the seventh Bishop of Rome in the second century. Tradition attributes to him the establishment of the Lenten fast before Pascha.

He suffered martyrdom under the Emperor Hadrian.
2-22.name: Telesphoros of Rome

2-22.bio:
St. Ariston was Bishop of Arsinoe in the region of Paphos in Cyprus at the end of the fourth and beginning of the fifth century. He was known for his miracles and his care for his flock.

He reposed in peace and is honoured among the holy hierarchs of Cyprus.
2-22.desc: St. Ariston the Wonderworker, Bishop of Arsinoe in Cyprus.
2-22.name: Ariston of Arsinoe

2-23.bio:
St. Polycarp was Bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of St. John the Theologian, a living link between the apostles and the generations that followed. He shepherded his church for many decades, and in extreme old age was arrested during a persecution in the second century. Urged to deny Christ, he answered that in eighty-six years the Lord had done him no wrong, and he could not blaspheme his King.

He was burned at the stake, and the account of his martyrdom, written by his church, is among the treasures of early Christianity. He is commemorated on February 23.
2-23.desc: Bishop of Smyrna, disciple of John the Theologian.
2-23.name: Polykarpos

2-23.bio:
St. Gorgonia was the daughter of St. Gregory the Elder and St. Nonna, and the sister of St. Gregory the Theologian, who delivered a funeral oration in her praise. A married woman and mother, she lived a life of prayer, fasting and charity, opening her home to the poor.

Tradition relates that she was healed of a serious illness by touching the holy altar. She reposed in peace in the fourth century.
2-23.desc: Righteous Gorgonia, sister of St. Gregory the Theologian.
2-23.name: Gorgonia

2-23.bio:
St. Damian became a monk at the Monastery of Esphigmenou on Mount Athos in his youth and was an example to the brethren. He later withdrew to live in stillness on the mountain of Samareia and in caves, struggling in prayer.

Tradition relates that a heavenly fragrance filled the area at the time of his repose in the thirteenth century.
2-23.desc: Venerable Damian, hesychast of the Monastery of Esphigmenou on Mount Athos.
2-23.name: Damian of Esphigmenou

2-23.bio:
St. Lazaros was a priest from Tripolis in the Peloponnese, born to pious parents. His service and synaxarion are preserved in a manuscript of the Monastery of Vatopedi on Mount Athos.

He confessed Christ before the Turks and received the crown of martyrdom.
2-23.desc: New Hieromartyr Lazaros, priest of Tripolis in the Peloponnese.
2-23.name: Lazaros of Tripolis

2-23.bio:
These fifth-century ascetics of Syria are described by Theodoret of Cyrrhus. John lived for twenty-five years on a hillside in the open, eating bread and salt; Moses, Antiochos and Antoninos followed similar lives of extreme self-denial.

All reposed in peace, honoured among the great ascetics of the Syrian desert.
2-23.desc: Venerable John, Moses, Antiochos and Antoninos, ascetics of the Syrian desert.
2-23.name: John, Moses, Antiochos and Antoninos

2-23.bio:
St. Zebinas lived to a great age on a mountain in Syria, standing in prayer day and night. His disciple Polychronios carried a heavy oak root as a self-imposed burden, and in turn taught Damian and Moses, who imitated his austerity.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus records their lives; they reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-23.desc: Venerable Zebinas, Polychronios, Damian and Moses, ascetics of Syria.
2-23.name: Zebinas, Polychronios, Damian and Moses

2-24.bio:
This feast commemorates the First and Second Findings of the honorable head of St. John the Forerunner. According to tradition, after the Baptist was beheaded by Herod his head was hidden, and in later generations it was revealed and recovered by the faithful; in times of persecution it was concealed again and found anew, each recovery received with rejoicing and accompanied by healings.

The Church keeps this commemoration on February 24, honoring the relics of the greatest of the prophets. The feast bears witness to the Orthodox veneration of holy relics, through which the grace of God that dwelt in the saints continues to work.
2-24.desc: First and Second Finding of the Honorable Head of the Holy Forerunner.
2-24.name: Finding of the Head of St. John the Baptist

2-24.bio:
St. Erasmus was a monk of the Kiev Caves who spent his entire fortune on the adornment of the monastery church. Later tempted by despair over his lost wealth, he fell ill, but was consoled by a vision of the Theotokos assuring him that his offering was accepted.

He repented, received the great schema and reposed in peace in the twelfth century.
2-24.desc: Venerable Erasmus of the Kiev Near Caves.
2-24.name: Erasmus of the Kiev Caves

2-24.bio:
St. John was born in Sicily to a Christian mother held captive by the Saracens and escaped to Calabria, where he became a monk in the Greek monastery of Stilo. Tradition relates that he miraculously harvested a field for the peasants during a storm, earning the name Harvester.

He reposed in peace in the eleventh century, and his monastery in Calabria is still called by his name.
2-24.desc: Venerable John the Harvester of Calabria.
2-24.name: John the Harvester

2-24.bio:
St. Ethelbert was King of Kent when St. Augustine and his monks arrived from Rome in 597. He received them kindly, was baptised, and allowed the free preaching of the Gospel, founding churches at Canterbury and elsewhere.

He reposed in 616 and is honoured as the first Christian king of the English.
2-24.desc: St. Ethelbert, King of Kent, first Christian king of the English.
2-24.name: Ethelbert of Kent

2-24.bio:
St. Boisil was prior and later abbot of the monastery of Melrose in the seventh century, renowned for his holiness and his gift of prophecy. He received the young St. Cuthbert into the monastery and was his teacher.

He foretold his own death from the plague and reposed in peace, having spent his last days reading the Gospel of John with his disciple.
2-24.desc: Venerable Boisil, Abbot of Melrose in Scotland, teacher of St. Cuthbert.
2-24.name: Boisil of Melrose

2-25.bio:
St. Tarasios was Patriarch of Constantinople at the end of the eighth century. A layman of high imperial office renowned for learning and virtue, he was raised to the patriarchal throne at a time when the Church was torn by the iconoclast heresy, and he accepted on the condition that the veneration of the holy icons be restored.

He presided over the Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 787, which vindicated the icons, and he shepherded the Church with charity toward the poor until his peaceful repose. He is commemorated on February 25.
2-25.name: Tarasios

2-25.bio:
St. Riginos was born in Livadeia in Boeotia in the fourth century and, having received both secular and Christian education, was made Bishop of Skopelos. He took part in the Council of Sardica in defence of the Orthodox faith against the Arians.

Under the Emperor Julian the Apostate he was arrested and beheaded on Skopelos, where he is honoured as the island's patron saint.
2-25.name: Riginos of Skopelos

2-25.bio:
St. Alexander was a soldier who confessed Christ during the persecution of Maximian and was led from city to city in Thrace, enduring tortures at each place.

He was finally beheaded at Drizipara, and a church was later built over his tomb.
2-25.desc: Holy Martyr Alexander of Drizipara in Thrace.
2-25.name: Alexander of Drizipara

2-25.bio: St. Antonios confessed Christ and was put to death by fire. The Synaxaria record only the fact of his martyrdom.
2-25.desc: Holy Martyr Antonios, who was burned for Christ.
2-25.name: Antonios the Martyr

2-25.bio: St. Theodore took up the ascetic path of foolishness for Christ's sake, hiding his virtue under the appearance of madness and enduring mockery for the Lord. He reposed in peace.
2-25.name: Theodore the Fool-for-Christ

2-25.bio: St. Markellos was Bishop of Solea in Cyprus and is honoured among the holy hierarchs of the island. Tradition relates that he shepherded his flock in holiness and reposed in peace.
2-25.desc: St. Markellos, Bishop of Solea in Cyprus.
2-25.name: Markellos of Solea

2-26.bio:
St. Porphyrios was Bishop of Gaza at the turn of the fifth century. Born in Thessalonica, he lived as an ascetic in Egypt and the Holy Land before being called, against his desire, to the episcopate of Gaza, a city then still devoted to idols.

With patience and courage he labored to turn the city to Christ, obtaining the closing of its pagan temples and raising a great church in their place, while caring tenderly for the poor. He reposed in peace after many years of toil. He is commemorated on February 26.
2-26.name: Porphyrios

2-26.bio:
St. Photini is the Samaritan woman of the Gospel of John who met Christ at Jacob's well and, having received from Him the living water, brought her whole city to believe in Him. After Pentecost she preached the Gospel in many lands together with her sons and sisters.

Tradition relates that she was brought before the Emperor Nero in Rome, converted his daughter, and after many tortures was thrown into a well, receiving the crown of martyrdom in the first century.
2-26.desc: Great Martyr Photini the Samaritan Woman, Equal-to-the-Apostles, who spoke with Christ at the well.
2-26.name: Photini the Samaritan Woman

2-26.bio:
St. Photini's five sisters, Anatole, Photo, Photis, Paraskevi and Kyriaki, and her sons Victor, called Photinos, and Joses, shared her missionary labours and her sufferings in Rome under Nero. The duke Sebastian, converted through Victor, was martyred with them.

All received the crown of martyrdom in the first century and are commemorated together with St. Photini.
2-26.desc: Sts. Anatole, Photo, Photis, Paraskevi and Kyriaki, sisters of St. Photini, her sons Victor and Joses, and the duke Sebastian.
2-26.greek: Ανατολή, Φωτώ, Φωτίς, Παρασκευή, Κυριακή, Βίκτωρ και Ιωσής
2-26.name: Companions of Photini

2-26.bio:
St. John was born in Galata in Constantinople and worked as a skilled cabinetmaker in the Sultan's palace and for other Turkish officials. When he spoke openly about the Christian faith to a young Muslim he had taken on as apprentice, he was denounced and pressed to embrace Islam.

He refused, endured imprisonment and torture, and was beheaded in Constantinople in 1575.
2-26.desc: New Martyr John Kalfas the cabinetmaker of Galata, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-26.name: John Kalfas

2-26.bio:
Theokletos was a sorcerer who was sent to poison St. Photini and her companions in Rome. Seeing that the poison did them no harm, he came to believe in Christ and was baptised.

He was beheaded for his confession, receiving the crown of martyrdom in the first century.
2-26.desc: Holy Martyr Theokletos, the former sorcerer who believed through St. Photini.
2-26.name: Theokletos the Martyr

2-26.bio:
St. Sebastian founded a monastery of the Transfiguration near the river Sokhota in the Yaroslavl region, where the monks supported themselves by the labour of their hands. He was known for his humility and ascetic life.

He reposed in peace at the beginning of the sixteenth century.
2-26.desc: Venerable Sebastian of Poshekhonye, founder of the Transfiguration Monastery.
2-26.name: Sebastian of Poshekhonye

2-27.bio:
St. Prokopios of the Dekapolis was a monk of the eighth century who lived the ascetic life in fasting, vigil, and prayer. When the iconoclast heresy arose under the emperors who warred against the holy images, he stood forth as a confessor, defending the veneration of the icons of Christ and His saints, and suffering persecution for the truth.

Having endured to the end, he reposed in peace, honored by the Church among the confessors of Orthodoxy. He is commemorated on February 27.
2-27.name: Prokopios Dekapolis

2-27.bio:
St. Ephraim was born in Ampelochori near Thebes in 1912 and baptised Evangelos. In 1933 he went to the desert of Katounakia on Mount Athos, where he was tonsured and ordained priest, and became a close disciple of St. Joseph the Hesychast, who taught him the way of the prayer of the heart.

Renowned for his obedience and for the grace of his liturgical celebration, he guided many pilgrims and reposed in 1998; he was glorified by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 2020.
2-27.desc: Venerable Ephraim of Katounakia, Athonite elder and disciple of St. Joseph the Hesychast.
2-27.name: Ephraim of Katounakia

2-27.bio:
St. Elias came from Kryoneri near Trebizond in Pontus and was the son of the priest Constantine. Seized by the Turks, he was tortured at the harbour of Trebizond and refused to deny Christ.

He was hanged in 1749, and the Christians buried his relics at the Monastery of Theoskepastos.
2-27.desc: New Martyr Elias of Trebizond, son of a priest, hanged for his faith.
2-27.name: Elias of Trebizond

2-27.bio:
Gelasios was an actor in Heliopolis who, mocking the Christian mysteries on stage, was plunged into a tub of water in imitation of baptism. Coming out, he declared that he had seen the glory of God and was now a Christian.

Enraged, the pagan crowd dragged him out and stoned him, and he received the crown of martyrdom in the third century.
2-27.desc: Holy Martyr Gelasios the actor, who believed while mocking baptism.
2-27.name: Gelasios the Mime

2-27.bio:
St. Thalelaios came from Cilicia and lived as a hermit near Gabala in Syria on the site of a former pagan shrine. He built himself a tiny cage-like cell in which he could neither stand nor lie straight, and remained in it for many years in prayer.

His gentleness and his miracles brought many pagans of the region to Christ. He reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-27.desc: Venerable Thalelaios of Cilicia, hermit near Gabala in Syria.
2-27.name: Thalelaios the Hermit

2-27.bio:
St. Raphael was born in Syria in 1860 to a devout Damascene family and studied at the theological school of Halki. He served the Antiochian Church in Russia before being sent to America in 1895 to care for the scattered Arab Orthodox faithful.

Consecrated Bishop of Brooklyn in 1904, the first Orthodox bishop consecrated in America, he founded parishes across the continent and reposed in 1915.
2-27.desc: St. Raphael Hawaweeny, Bishop of Brooklyn, shepherd of the Orthodox in America.
2-27.name: Raphael of Brooklyn

2-27.bio:
St. Stephen was a courtier under the Emperor Maurice who used his wealth to found a hospice for the elderly in Constantinople, devoting himself to the care of strangers and the poor.

He reposed in peace in the early seventh century.
2-27.desc: Righteous Stephen of Constantinople, founder of a hospice for the aged.
2-27.name: Stephen of Constantinople

2-28.bio:
St. Basil the Confessor was a monk of the eighth century and the companion in asceticism of St. Prokopios of the Dekapolis. When the iconoclast heresy broke out, he stood with his fellow ascetic in defense of the veneration of the holy icons, and for this confession he endured imprisonment and ill-treatment.

When the persecution abated he returned to his labors of fasting and prayer, guiding others in the ascetic life until his peaceful repose. He is commemorated on February 28.
2-28.desc: Venerable Basil the Confessor, companion of St. Procopius.
2-28.name: Basil the Confessor

2-28.bio:
St. Kyranna was born in the village of Avyssoka, the present-day Ossa near Thessaloniki, to devout parents, and was renowned for her beauty. A janissary tax collector who desired her tried with gifts, flattery and threats to make her renounce her faith and marry him.

When she refused, she was imprisoned in Thessaloniki and beaten daily until she died of her wounds in 1751; tradition relates that a heavenly light filled the prison at her death.
2-28.desc: New Martyr Kyranna of Ossa near Thessaloniki.
2-28.name: Kyranna of Ossa

2-28.bio:
St. Proterios was a presbyter of Alexandria who opposed the Monophysite errors of the Patriarch Dioscoros and was chosen to succeed him after the Council of Chalcedon. The followers of Dioscoros rose against him with violence.

He was murdered by a Monophysite mob in the baptistery of the church in 457 and is honoured as a martyr for the Orthodox faith.
2-28.name: Proterios of Alexandria

2-28.bio:
Sts. Marana and Kyra were noblewomen of Beroea in Syria who renounced their wealth and lived for over forty years in a roofless enclosure outside the city, wearing chains and keeping silence except during the Paschal season.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who visited them, records their life; they reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-28.desc: Venerable Marana and Kyra, ascetics of Beroea in Syria.
2-28.name: Marana and Kyra

2-28.bio:
St. Nestor was Bishop of Magydos in Pamphylia during the persecution of Decius. Arrested while at prayer, he was brought to Perge and refused to sacrifice to the idols.

He was tortured and crucified in the mid-third century, receiving the crown of martyrdom.
2-28.desc: Hieromartyr Nestor, Bishop of Magydos in Pamphylia.
2-28.name: Nestor of Magydos

2-28.bio:
The Apostles Nymphas and Euboulos were disciples of the Apostle Paul. Nymphas, whose house at Laodicea served as a church, is greeted in the Epistle to the Colossians; Euboulos is mentioned in the Second Epistle to Timothy as being with Paul in Rome.

Both laboured in spreading the Gospel and reposed in peace.
2-28.desc: Holy Apostles Nymphas and Euboulos of the Seventy, disciples of St. Paul.
2-28.name: Nymphas and Euboulos

2-28.bio:
St. Barsos, also known as John-Barsanouphios, was a Palestinian monk who reluctantly accepted consecration as Bishop of Damascus. Longing for stillness, he later laid aside his office and returned to the solitary life.

He reposed in peace, honoured among the holy hierarchs of Syria.
2-28.name: Barsos of Damascus

2-29.bio:
St. John Cassian the Roman was a monk of the late fourth and early fifth centuries. In his youth he journeyed with his friend Germanos to the monasteries of Palestine and to the great elders of the Egyptian desert, gathering their wisdom, and later he settled in Gaul, near Marseilles, where he founded monasteries for men and for women.

His writings, the Institutes and the Conferences, carried the teaching of the desert fathers to the Christian West and remain classics of the spiritual life. His memory is kept on February 29, and in ordinary years on February 28.
2-29.name: John Cassian the Roman

2-29.bio:
St. Theoktiristos was abbot of the Monastery of Pelekete in Bithynia during the iconoclast persecution of the Emperor Constantine Copronymus. He and his monks were seized for their veneration of the holy icons.

He was tortured and burned with boiling pitch, receiving the crown of martyrdom in the eighth century.
2-29.desc: Hieromartyr Theoktiristos, Abbot of the Pelekete Monastery, who suffered under the iconoclasts.
2-29.name: Theoktiristos of Pelekete

2-29.bio:
St. Leo was a monk of Cappadocia who, when three sick monks were carried off by Saracen raiders, offered himself in their place as a captive.

Weakened by the hardships of the march through the desert, he died on the way, laying down his life for his brethren.
2-29.desc: Venerable Leo of Cappadocia, who gave himself as a ransom for captive monks.
2-29.name: Leo of Cappadocia

2-29.bio:
St. Germanos was born in the fourth century in Dacia Pontica, the present-day Dobrogea in Romania, and was a kinsman and lifelong companion of St. John Cassian. Together they visited the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine and later lived in Constantinople under St. John Chrysostom.

He accompanied Cassian to Rome to plead the cause of the exiled Chrysostom and reposed in peace in the early fifth century.
2-29.desc: Venerable Germanos of Dacia Pontica, companion of St. John Cassian.
2-29.name: Germanos of Dobrogea

2-29.bio:
St. Oswald was of Danish descent and became a monk at Fleury in France before returning to England, where he was made Bishop of Worcester and later Archbishop of York in the tenth century. With Sts. Dunstan and Ethelwold he restored monastic life in England.

He was known for his humility and his daily washing of the feet of the poor, and reposed in 992, a pre-schism saint of the undivided Church.
2-29.desc: St. Oswald, Bishop of Worcester and Archbishop of York.
2-29.name: Oswald of Worcester

2-3.bio:
The righteous Simeon the God-Receiver was the elder to whom it was revealed by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord. When the infant Jesus was brought to the Temple forty days after His birth, Simeon received Him into his arms and blessed God with the prayer sung at every Vespers: Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace.

He is honored on the day after the feast of the Meeting of the Lord, together with the Prophetess Anna who also bore witness to the Child. His memory is kept on February 3.
2-3.desc: The Elder Simeon who received the infant Christ in the Temple.
2-3.name: Simeon the God-Receiver

2-3.bio:
The Gospel of Luke relates that Anna, daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, was a widow of great age who never left the Temple but served God with fasting and prayer night and day.

When the Christ Child was brought to the Temple she gave thanks to God and spoke of Him to all who awaited the redemption of Jerusalem. She is honoured together with the righteous Simeon on the day after the Presentation.
2-3.desc: Righteous Anna the Prophetess, who greeted the infant Christ in the Temple.
2-3.name: Anna the Prophetess

2-3.bio:
The brothers Stamatios and John, and their companion Nicholas, came from the island of Spetses. Tradition relates that they travelled to Chios on business and were denounced to the Turkish authorities after a dispute.

Refusing to renounce Christ, they were beheaded in Chios in the early nineteenth century and are honoured as the patron martyrs of Spetses.
2-3.desc: New Martyrs Stamatios and John, brothers, with their companion Nicholas, of Spetses.
2-3.name: Stamatios, John and Nicholas of Spetses

2-3.bio:
The Prophet Azariah, son of Oded, is mentioned in the Second Book of Chronicles. Moved by the Spirit of God he went out to meet King Asa of Judah and exhorted him and the people to seek the Lord and put away idolatry.

The king took courage from his words and renewed the covenant of the people with God.
2-3.desc: Holy Prophet Azariah, son of Oded, who called King Asa to faithfulness.
2-3.name: Azariah the Prophet

2-3.bio:
Sts. Adrian and Euboulos came from Baneas and travelled to Caesarea in Palestine to visit the imprisoned confessors during the persecution of Diocletian. Arrested by the governor Firmilian, they confessed Christ openly.

Adrian was thrown to a lion and then slain by the sword; Euboulos suffered the same death a few days later, in the early fourth century.
2-3.desc: Holy Martyrs Adrian and Euboulos of Caesarea in Palestine.
2-3.name: Adrian and Euboulos of Caesarea

2-3.bio:
St. Nicholas, born Ivan Kasatkin in Russia in the nineteenth century, went to Japan as a young priest-monk and devoted his life to preaching the Gospel there. He mastered the Japanese language, translated the Scriptures and services, and founded the Orthodox Church of Japan.

He was consecrated bishop and later archbishop of Tokyo, and reposed in 1912, revered by Japanese and Russians alike as an apostle of Japan.
2-3.desc: St. Nicholas Kasatkin, Equal-to-the-Apostles, Enlightener of Japan.
2-3.name: Nicholas of Japan

2-3.bio:
St. Blaise was a shepherd of Caesarea in Cappadocia. During a persecution the pagans sought him as a Christian; when he learned of it he surrendered himself and confessed Christ before the governor.

He was cruelly tortured and gave up his soul to God, receiving the crown of martyrdom in the third century.
2-3.desc: Holy Martyr Blaise the Shepherd of Caesarea in Cappadocia.
2-3.name: Blaise the Shepherd

2-4.bio:
St. Isidore of Pelusium was an ascetic of Egypt in the fifth century, who lived in monastic retirement near the city of Pelusium at the mouth of the Nile. A man of wide learning and deep devotion to the Holy Scriptures, he revered the teaching of St. John Chrysostom and followed his example of bold and clear instruction.

He is remembered above all for his letters, written by the thousands to people of every rank, expounding the Scriptures and correcting faults with wisdom and charity. He is commemorated on February 4.
2-4.name: Isidore of Pelusium

2-4.bio:
St. Abramios was Bishop of Arbela in Persia during the persecution of Christians under King Shapur II. Commanded to renounce Christ and worship the sun, he refused, declaring that he would never abandon the true God.

After being tortured he was beheaded in the fourth century, one of the many martyrs of the Persian Church.
2-4.desc: Hieromartyr Abramios, Bishop of Arbela in Persia.
2-4.name: Abramios of Arbela

2-4.bio:
St. Nicholas was born in Crete and as a boy was sent to Constantinople, where he entered the Monastery of Studion under St. Theodore the Studite. He shared in the sufferings of his abbot during the iconoclast persecution, enduring imprisonment and exile.

After the restoration of the icons he became abbot of Studion, and reposed in peace in the ninth century.
2-4.desc: Venerable Nicholas the Confessor, Abbot of the Studion Monastery.
2-4.name: Nicholas the Studite

2-4.bio:
St. Joseph came from Aleppo in Syria. Because of his piety he was falsely accused by Muslims of having promised to convert to Islam. Before the judge he remained unshaken in his faith and boldly confessed Christ.

When flattery and threats failed to move him, he was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom in the seventeenth century.
2-4.desc: New Martyr Joseph of Aleppo, slandered and beheaded for his faith.
2-4.name: Joseph of Aleppo

2-4.bio:
St. George, son of Great Prince Vsevolod, ruled Vladimir in the thirteenth century and was known for his piety, his building of churches and his care for the poor. He founded the city of Nizhny Novgorod.

When the Tatar hordes invaded Russia he led his army against them and was killed in battle in 1238; his relics were later found incorrupt.
2-4.desc: Right-believing Great Prince George of Vladimir, who fell defending his people from the Tatars.
2-4.name: George of Vladimir

2-4.bio:
St. Cyril was born near Novgorod and in his youth secretly left home to become a monk under St. Cornelius of Komel. After years of ascetic struggle he settled on an island in the Red Lake, where he founded a monastery in honour of the Resurrection.

He was granted the gifts of clairvoyance and healing and reposed in peace in the sixteenth century.
2-4.desc: Venerable Cyril the Wonderworker, Abbot of Novoezersk in Novgorod.
2-4.name: Cyril of Novoezersk

2-5.bio:
St. Agatha was a virgin martyr of Sicily who suffered for Christ during the persecution of Decius in the third century. Of noble birth, she consecrated herself to the Lord, and when she refused the advances of the pagan governor she was subjected to cruel tortures, which she endured with unshaken faith, dying in prison from her sufferings.

She is greatly venerated in Sicily, above all in Catania, whose people have long sought her protection, and her name is honored throughout the Church, East and West. Her feast is kept on February 5.
2-5.name: Agatha

2-5.bio:
St. Theodosios came from a noble family of Antioch and left the world to live as a hermit on a mountain near Rhosos in Cilicia, wearing chains and working with his hands. Many disciples gathered around him and he founded a monastery.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus records his life; he reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-5.desc: Venerable Theodosios of Antioch, ascetic of the mountains of Cilicia.
2-5.name: Theodosios of Antioch

2-5.bio:
St. Polyeuktos was a monk of Constantinople known for his learning and ascetic life who was raised to the patriarchal throne in the tenth century. He was fearless in rebuking emperors and firm in defending the canons of the Church.

During his patriarchate the Russian princess Olga was baptised in Constantinople. He reposed in peace after governing the Church for many years.
2-5.name: Polyeuktos of Constantinople

2-5.bio:
St. Antonios was born in Athens to poor parents and as a boy was put to work for Turkish masters, who sold him from one owner to another and pressed him to renounce his faith. He held fast to Christ through every hardship.

Later, working in Constantinople, he was falsely accused of having embraced and abandoned Islam, and after refusing to deny Christ he was beheaded in the eighteenth century.
2-5.desc: New Martyr Antonios of Athens, who suffered in Constantinople.
2-5.name: Antonios the Athenian

2-5.bio:
St. Theodosios was born in the seventeenth century to a noble family of Podolia and educated at the Kiev academy. He became a monk, served as abbot of several monasteries, and was consecrated Archbishop of Chernigov.

He was known for his humility, his generosity and his care for the clergy and the poor; after his repose many miracles were worked at his relics.
2-5.desc: St. Theodosios, Archbishop of Chernigov, wonderworker.
2-5.name: Theodosios of Chernigov

2-6.bio:
St. Bukolos was a disciple of St. John the Theologian, who consecrated him the first Bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor. In the earliest days of the Church he shepherded his flock amid the surrounding paganism with gentleness and wisdom, bringing many to the faith of Christ.

Before his peaceful repose he consecrated as his successor St. Polycarp, the future hieromartyr, thus handing on the apostolic faith he had received from the Beloved Disciple. He is commemorated on February 6.
2-6.desc: Bishop of Smyrna and disciple of John the Theologian.
2-6.name: Bukolos of Smyrna

2-6.bio:
St. Photios was born in Constantinople in the ninth century to a devout family that had suffered for the holy icons. A man of immense learning, he served in the imperial administration before being raised to the patriarchal throne. He sent missionaries to the Slavs, among them Sts. Cyril and Methodios, and defended the Orthodox faith against the innovations of the Latins.

He was twice deposed and exiled through political intrigue, and reposed in exile, leaving a vast body of theological and literary writings. He is honoured as one of the great Fathers and Confessors of the Church.
2-6.desc: St. Photios the Great, Patriarch of Constantinople, Confessor and Pillar of Orthodoxy.
2-6.name: Photios the Great

2-6.bio:
St. Julian was a physician of Emesa in Syria who healed both body and soul, bringing many to faith in Christ. During the persecution of Maximian he visited the imprisoned bishop Silvanos and his companions and encouraged them.

Denounced as a Christian, he was tortured and finally put to death with nails driven into his head and limbs, in the early fourth century.
2-6.desc: Holy Martyr Julian the physician of Emesa in Syria.
2-6.name: Julian of Emesa

2-6.bio:
St. Fausta was a young Christian maiden of Cyzicus who was arrested under Maximian and handed over to the pagan priest Evilasios for torture. Amazed at her endurance, Evilasios came to believe in Christ and was tortured in turn.

The governor Maximos, seeing their steadfastness, also confessed Christ, and all three received the crown of martyrdom together.
2-6.desc: Virgin Martyr Fausta of Cyzicus, with Evilasios and Maximos whom she converted.
2-6.name: Fausta, Evilasios and Maximos

2-6.bio:
St. Barsanouphios, an Egyptian by birth, lived as a recluse at the monastery of Abba Seridos near Gaza in the sixth century, communicating with the world only through letters. His disciple John, called the Prophet for his gift of foresight, lived in a nearby cell.

Their letters of spiritual counsel, answering questions from monks and laypeople, survive as one of the treasures of Orthodox ascetic literature.
2-6.desc: Venerable Barsanouphios the Great and John the Prophet, elders of Gaza.
2-6.name: Barsanouphios and John

2-6.bio:
St. Dorothea was a devout maiden of Caesarea in Cappadocia who was arrested during the persecution of Diocletian. Two sisters who had lapsed from the faith were sent to sway her, but she brought them back to Christ and they were martyred with her.

Tradition relates that the lawyer Theophilos mocked her, asking her to send him fruit and flowers from paradise; a child brought them to him after her death, and he too confessed Christ and was martyred.
2-6.desc: Virgin Martyr Dorothea of Caesarea in Cappadocia, with Christina, Kallista and Theophilos.
2-6.name: Dorothea of Caesarea

2-7.bio:
St. Parthenius was Bishop of Lampsakos, on the Hellespont in Asia Minor, in the fourth century, in the days of St. Constantine the Great. The son of a deacon, he was a simple fisherman in his youth, giving to the poor what he earned, and after his consecration he labored to turn his region from idolatry to Christ.

He was renowned as a wonderworker, healing the sick and delivering the afflicted through his prayers, and he reposed in peace. He is commemorated on February 7.
2-7.name: Parthenius

2-7.bio:
St. Luke was born in the tenth century to a family of farmers in central Greece and from childhood gave away his food and clothing to the poor. He became a monk and struggled in several places before settling on Mount Steirion near Delphi, where disciples gathered around him.

He was granted the gifts of prophecy and healing, and after his repose the great monastery of Hosios Loukas rose over his tomb, where his relics are venerated to this day.
2-7.desc: Venerable Luke of Hellas, ascetic of Mount Steirion, founder of the Monastery of Hosios Loukas.
2-7.name: Luke of Steirion

2-7.bio:
St. George was born in the village of Alikianos in Crete, the son of a priest. During the Cretan uprising of 1866 he was captured by the Turks together with other insurgents and pressed with threats and torture to change his faith in order to save his life.

He confessed Christ with courage and was put to death, receiving the crown of martyrdom.
2-7.desc: New Martyr George Divolis of Alikianos in Crete.
2-7.name: George of Alikianos

2-7.bio:
The 1,003 martyrs were the household servants of four Christian officials of Nicomedia who had been put to death under Diocletian. Following the example of their masters, they presented themselves to the emperor and confessed Christ together with their wives and children.

All were slain by the sword in the early fourth century.
2-7.desc: The Holy 1,003 Martyrs of Nicomedia, servants of four martyred dignitaries.
2-7.name: 1,003 Martyrs of Nicomedia

2-7.bio: St. Aprion is commemorated as a bishop of the Church in Cyprus who shepherded his flock in holiness and reposed in peace. Few details of his life have been preserved in the Synaxaria.
2-7.name: Aprion of Cyprus

2-7.bio: St. Theopemptos and his companions confessed Christ before their persecutors and were beheaded. The Synaxaria preserve only the fact of their martyrdom.
2-7.desc: Holy Martyr Theopemptos and those with him, who suffered by the sword.
2-7.name: Theopemptos and his Companions

2-8.bio:
St. Theodore Stratelates, the Commander, was a general in the Roman army, admired for his bravery and his noble bearing. A Christian, he openly confessed Christ before the Emperor Licinius during the persecutions of the early fourth century, and for this he was subjected to cruel tortures and finally beheaded at Heraclea.

He is honored as a Great Martyr and, together with St. Theodore the Recruit, is one of the most beloved warrior saints of the Church, a patron of soldiers. He is commemorated on February 8.
2-8.desc: Great Martyr Theodore Stratelates the Commander.
2-8.name: Theodore Stratelates

2-8.bio:
The Prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah, was of the tribe of Levi and prophesied in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian captivity, encouraging the people to rebuild the Temple. His book contains visions and prophecies of the coming Messiah, including His entry into Jerusalem on a donkey.

He reposed in peace at a great age and was buried near Jerusalem.
2-8.desc: Holy Prophet Zechariah, one of the Twelve Minor Prophets.
2-8.name: Zechariah the Prophet

2-8.bio:
St. Sava II was born Predislav, son of King Stefan the First-Crowned and nephew of St. Sava of Serbia. Following his uncle's example he became a monk on Mount Athos and made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

He was chosen Archbishop of Serbia in the thirteenth century and governed the Church with humility and zeal, reposing in peace.
2-8.desc: St. Sava II, Archbishop of Serbia, nephew of St. Sava.
2-8.name: Sava II of Serbia

2-8.bio:
The sisters Martha and Mary devoted their lives to spreading the Christian faith among women. When a pagan governor passed by their house they cried out that they were Christians, and their young brother Lycarion, a monk, joined them in their confession.

The governor tried to spare them because of their youth, but they refused to deny Christ and all three were crucified and slain by the sword.
2-8.desc: Virgin Martyrs Martha and Mary, and their brother the monk-martyr Lycarion, in Egypt.
2-8.name: Martha, Mary and Lycarion

2-8.bio: Sts. Nikephoros and Stephen confessed Christ before their persecutors and were beheaded. The Synaxaria record only the fact of their martyrdom.
2-8.desc: Holy Martyrs Nikephoros and Stephen, who suffered by the sword.
2-8.name: Nikephoros and Stephen the Martyrs

2-8.bio: St. Macarios was Bishop of Paphos in Cyprus and is honoured among the holy hierarchs of the island. Tradition relates that he shepherded his flock with holiness and reposed in peace.
2-8.desc: St. Macarios, Bishop of Paphos in Cyprus.
2-8.name: Macarios of Paphos

2-9.bio:
St. Nicephorus was a Christian of Antioch in the third century, remembered for a martyrdom born of humility. He had quarreled with a priest named Sapricius, and though Nicephorus repeatedly sought forgiveness, the priest refused to be reconciled. When persecution came, Sapricius was led to execution as a confessor, yet, devoid of love, he denied Christ at the last moment.

Nicephorus, who had begged his forgiveness even on the road, then confessed Christ himself and was beheaded, receiving the crown the unforgiving priest had lost. His story teaches that martyrdom without love profits nothing. He is commemorated on February 9.
2-9.name: Nicephorus

2-9.bio:
Sts. Marcellus, Philagrios and Pancratios were disciples of the Apostle Peter, who consecrated them bishops and sent them to preach: Marcellus to Sicily, Philagrios to Cyprus and Pancratios to Taormina.

All three laboured to bring the pagans to Christ and sealed their apostolic work with martyrdom in the first century.
2-9.desc: Hieromartyrs Marcellus of Sicily, Philagrios of Cyprus and Pancratios of Taormina, disciples of the Apostle Peter.
2-9.name: Marcellus, Philagrios and Pancratios

2-9.bio:
St. Romanos came from Rhosos in Cilicia and lived as a hermit in a cave near Antioch, wearing heavy chains beneath a hair shirt and never lighting a fire. Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who knew him, records his life.

He was granted the gift of healing, and many childless couples received children through his prayers. He reposed in peace in the fifth century.
2-9.desc: Venerable Romanos of Cilicia, wonderworker, hermit near Antioch.
2-9.name: Romanos of Cilicia

2-9.bio:
St. Peter of Damascus was a priest and later bishop who enlightened the faithful with his preaching and by his own blameless example. He is the author of the ascetic works preserved in the Philokalia.

Tradition relates that he rebuked the errors of the Muslims and Manichaeans, for which his tongue was cut out and he was exiled to Arabia, where he died a martyr.
2-9.desc: Hieromartyr Peter of Damascus, ascetic writer of the Philokalia.
2-9.name: Peter of Damascus

2-9.bio: Sts. Ammon and Alexander confessed Christ and endured martyrdom. The Synaxaria record only the fact of their death for the faith.
2-9.desc: Holy Martyrs Ammon and Alexander, who suffered for Christ.
2-9.name: Ammon and Alexander

2-9.bio:
St. Pancratios was a hieromonk of the Far Caves of the Kiev Caves Lavra who lived in seclusion. He healed the sick by fasting, prayer and anointing with holy oil.

He reposed in the thirteenth century and his relics rest in the Far Caves.
2-9.desc: Venerable Pancratios the Recluse, hieromonk of the Kiev Caves.
2-9.name: Pancratios of the Kiev Caves
